spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The source compresses a fluctuating singular-series discrepancy into one primitive f. Once centered by B/2 and integrated, the same arithmetic error can be moved through weighted integrals by parts and controlled by a single growth estimate.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Using Lemma 2.1, the source derives an average for epsilon(u), defines f(y) as the integral of epsilon(u)-B/2, and by integration by parts obtains a head identity for integral epsilon(u)u du and a tail identity for integral epsilon(u)/u^3 du.
directed.conceptual_reading: Centering removes the deterministic mean, and taking a primitive converts several discrete summatory errors into a reusable analytic remainder. Integration by parts then exposes boundary terms and shifts weight onto f.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The sequence of objects is the centered singular-series sum epsilon, its integrated remainder f, and weighted head/tail transforms. This is the arithmetic-to-analytic bridge later shared by multiple correction terms.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The bounds inherit the earlier singular-series estimates and ultimately the source's prime-pair hypothesis. This unit does not independently justify those inputs.
directed.uncertainty: Some exact coefficients are formula-layout-sensitive, but the definition of f, the integration-by-parts mechanism, and the stated growth orders are recoverable.

supported: The span derives an average for epsilon from Lemma 2.1, defines f(y) as the primitive of epsilon(u)-B/2, and uses integration by parts with Lemma 2.2 to obtain complementary head and tail identities.

inference: Treating f as a reusable analytic remainder is a substantive interpretation of its repeated appearance in the two weighted identities.

The plural claim about converting several discrete summatory errors overstates a span that begins with the already-defined epsilon.

revision_instructions: Describe dependence only on Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2 unless their hypotheses are explicitly supplied; narrow the conceptual claim to converting epsilon into a shared primitive remainder.
